subject: Pathology
summary: Pericardial disease includes inflammation, fluid accumulation, and constriction of the pericardium, which can impair cardiac filling and output. Prompt recognition of tamponade or constriction is essential to prevent death.

sections.p: Pericardial disease refers to any pathological process affecting the pericardial sac, ranging from acute pericarditis to chronic constriction. Diagnosis requires clinical suspicion, imaging, and ECG criteria.
b: Acute pericarditis: pleuritic chest pain, friction rub, diffuse ST‑elevation.
Tamponade: Beck's triad + pulsus paradoxus.
Constrictive pericarditis: pericardial thickening with restricted diastolic filling.

sections.p: Severity is staged by hemodynamic impact: uncomplicated pericarditis, effusive‑constrictive, tamponade, and chronic constriction.
b: Stage I – mild inflammation, no effusion.
Stage II – moderate effusion, no tamponade.
Stage III – tamponade physiology.
Stage IV – chronic constriction with fibrosis.

sections.p: Identify the underlying trigger to guide therapy; infectious and non‑infectious causes differ by region.
b: Viral (Coxsackie B) – most common worldwide.
Tuberculosis – prevalent in low‑resource settings.
Uremia – in patients with advanced renal failure.
Post‑myocardial infarction (Dressler) – weeks after MI.
Autoimmune (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis).
Trauma or cardiac surgery.

sections.p: Symptoms reflect irritation or compression of the heart.
b: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain improved by sitting up.
Fever, malaise in inflammatory forms.
Dyspnea, orthopnea when effusion enlarges.
Neck vein distension, hypotension in tamponade.
Peripheral edema and ascites in constriction.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Does the ECG show diffuse ST‑elevation or low voltage? Diffuse ST‑elevation supports acute pericarditis; low voltage suggests large effusion.
Is there an enlarged cardiac silhouette? A ‘water‑bottle’ heart indicates significant effusion.
Is there pericardial fluid and evidence of tamponade (right‑atrial collapse, respiratory variation)? Confirms effusion and hemodynamic impact.
Is pericardial thickening or calcification present? Helps diagnose constrictive pericarditis when echo is equivocal.
What is the fluid type (exudate vs transudate) and microbiology? Guides treatment for TB, bacterial, or malignant causes.
Are inflammatory markers elevated or is uremia present? Supports inflammatory vs uremic pericarditis.

sections.p: Recognize features that signal imminent collapse or chronic damage.
b: Rapidly enlarging effusion with hypotension.
Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg.
Persistent fever with positive TB culture.
Progressive dyspnea despite therapy.
Signs of constriction (Kussmaul’s sign, pericardial knock).

sections.p: Treat the cause first, then control inflammation and prevent hemodynamic compromise.
b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for viral or idiopathic pericarditis – reduce inflammation.
Colchicine added to NSAIDs – lowers recurrence, avoids steroids when possible.
Corticosteroids only for autoimmune or refractory cases – avoid early use due to higher recurrence.
Anti‑TB therapy for tuberculous pericarditis – standard 6‑month regimen.
Urgent pericardiocentesis for tamponade – relieve pressure.
Pericardiectomy for chronic constriction unresponsive to medical therapy.

sections.p: Monitor for recurrence, progression, and drug side effects.
b: Repeat echo 1–2 weeks after effusion drainage.
Serial ESR/CRP to gauge inflammation resolution.
Educate patients on early return if chest pain worsens or dyspnea recurs.
Vaccinate against influenza and COVID‑19 to reduce viral triggers.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic pericardial disease clinically or on imaging.
b: Myocardial infarction – both cause chest pain, but MI lacks friction rub and diffuse ST‑elevation.
Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic pain and tachycardia, but CT angiography shows emboli.
Pleural effusion – can cause dullness, but does not produce Beck’s triad.

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation that may delay correct diagnosis.
b: Normal ECG early in tamponade – rely on echo if suspicion high.
Low‑grade fever may be absent in TB pericarditis; consider epidemiology.
Elevated troponin can occur with pericarditis; do not assume MI without coronary assessment.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden hypotension with muffled heart sounds (tamponade).
Severe dyspnea or syncope on minimal exertion.
Persistent high fever with chest pain in TB‑endemic areas.

faq.q: Why does leaning forward relieve pericarditis pain?
faq.a: It reduces pressure of the inflamed pericardial layers against the chest wall, decreasing friction.
Yes, usually from uremia or hypo‑albuminemia; exudates suggest infection, malignancy, or TB.
Add colchicine to NSAIDs for acute pericarditis and for recurrent episodes to lower relapse risk.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis and how you would confirm tamponade.
List the most common causes of pericardial disease in a low‑resource setting and the first‑line treatment for each.
Explain the pathophysiology of pulsus paradoxus and its clinical significance.
